books.title: Ships and Boats
books.art_why: Covers ancient boats through modern ships, and early scenes predate photographs.

pages.text: Introduction Before there were cars, trains, or airplanes, boats were the fastest way to travel. They helped to shape history, leading explorers to new lands and spreading new ideas around the world. Ships and boats have changed a lot over the years but still have much in common with the earliest designs.
pages.brief: An early wooden boat carries explorers across open water toward a distant new land, while a later boat travels nearby on the same water, showing how ships changed over time yet still share the same basic design.

pages.text: Early Ships and Boats The first boats were carved from single wooden logs. These dugout canoes were used in rivers, lakes, and oceans around the world. People used long poles, paddles, or oars to move the canoes through the water. Paddles and oars are long pieces of wood with broad, flat ends. They push against the water to move the boat forward. Later, people began to make boats with wooden frames. They covered the frame with bark, reeds, or animal skins to keep out the water.
pages.brief: On a river, lake, or ocean, people paddle a dugout canoe carved from a single wooden log, using long paddles with broad, flat ends; nearby, a wooden frame boat is covered with bark, reeds, or animal skins.

pages.text: In the South Pacific, people were building boats that could sail well beyond the islands where they lived. People took two canoes and connected them using large wooden poles. This style of boat was called a catamaran. The catamaran could travel very fast. It also allowed safe travel from one island to another.
pages.brief: In the South Pacific, people build a fast catamaran by joining two canoes with large wooden poles. The double-hulled boat travels safely over the water from one island to another, carrying people beyond the islands where they live.

pages.text: Some frame ships, such as galleys, were much larger than log boats. Thousands of years ago, many groups of people around the Mediterranean Sea used galleys for trade and warfare. Galleys were frame ships covered with wood that carried many rowers. The largest galleys had hundreds of rowers sitting on several decks. Many galleys also had sails made from strong cloth. Sails could be used when the wind was blowing in the direction the ship was traveling.
pages.brief: On the Mediterranean Sea, a large wooden galley carries many rowers sitting on several decks, pulling long oars. A strong cloth sail rises above the frame ship, ready to catch the wind as the galley travels for trade and warfare.

pages.text: In time, boats and ships relied more and more on wind power. Sailboats could ships that relied on rowers for their power. The Vikings used wooden-framed longships to cross the sea to raid towns and villages on other coasts. Like galleys, longships had sails as well as oars. The Vikings could land by surprise anywhere along the coast, something that helped them in battle.
pages.brief: A Viking longship with a wooden frame crosses the sea, using both a sail and many oars. Vikings aboard the longship approach a coast, ready to land by surprise at towns and villages, a move that helped them in battle.

pages.text: Around 500 years ago, larger sailing ships began to be built. These sailing ships were able to cross the ocean. Famous explorers such as Ferdinand Magellan used sailing ships to travel from Europe to North and South America. Magellan was also the first captain to sail completely around the world.
pages.brief: Ferdinand Magellan stands on a large sailing ship crossing the ocean from Europe toward North and South America. The ship's cloth sails fill with wind as it travels, and Magellan becomes the first captain to sail completely around the world.

pages.text: Modern Ships and Boats When steam engines were invented, they were used in many boat and ship designs. Steamships did not depend on the wind for power. They could sail into the wind or even when there was no wind at all. Steamboats using paddlewheels became an important way to move quickly up and down rivers.
pages.brief: A steamboat with a paddlewheel moves quickly along a river, powered by a steam engine rather than the wind. Nearby, a steamship travels on open water, able to sail into the wind or even when no wind blows at all.

pages.text: Today, many boats are made of metal and plastic. Many ships and boats use electricity to turn their propellers. The propellers push the boat through the water. Some modern ships are very large. Cruise ships are like floating hotels. They can carry thousands of people all around the world. Huge tankers carry oil and gas over the ocean.
pages.brief: Today, boats made of metal and plastic use electricity to turn propellers that push them through the water. A huge cruise ship, like a floating hotel, carries thousands of people around the world, while a massive tanker carries oil and gas across the ocean.

pages.text: Some boats and ships are built to do special work. Tugboats push and pull larger ships in places where they can’t move themselves. Fireboats help put out fires on other ships. Ferryboats carry cars and people.
pages.brief: Special workboats are shown on the water: a tugboat pushes and pulls a larger ship where it cannot move itself, a fireboat helps put out fires on another ship, and a ferryboat carries cars and people across the water.

pages.text: Many countries use ships and boats, large and small, to defend their coasts. Submarines hide under the surface of the water. Aircraft carriers serve as floating runways and allow planes and helicopters to fly anywhere in the world.
pages.brief: A country's ships and boats defend its coast, large and small. A submarine hides under the surface of the water, while an aircraft carrier serves as a floating runway, allowing planes and helicopters to fly anywhere in the world from its deck.

pages.text: Although large, modern boats with propellers are everywhere today, people still use smaller boats for fishing, fun, and sport. It is almost impossible to look at a river, lake, or ocean and not see a variety of boats. Many smaller boats still use paddles, oars, or sails, just as the earliest boats did.
pages.brief: On a river, lake, or ocean, people use a variety of smaller boats for fishing, fun, and sport. Some boats still use paddles, oars, or sails, just as the earliest boats did, while large modern boats with propellers can also be seen nearby.

pages.text: Conclusion Ships and boats have played an important part in human history. For thousands of years, they have allowed people to explore their world. They are still an important way to move quickly over the water.
pages.brief: For thousands of years, ships and boats have carried people across the water to explore their world. A range of boats moves over the water, showing that ships and boats remain an important way to travel quickly over water.

books.title: Weird Bird Beaks
books.art_why: Real birds can be photographed today.

pages.text: Bearded Barbet I am a bearded barbet. I have a large, thick beak that has pointed parts on the bottom like sharp teeth. Hairlike feathers look like a beard on my beak. I live where it is dry in Africa, where I build my nest in a dead tree. I feed on fruit and sometimes on insects.
pages.brief: A bearded barbet in dry Africa has a large, thick beak with pointed parts underneath like sharp teeth. Hairlike feathers look like a beard on its beak. It builds its nest in a dead tree and feeds on fruit and sometimes insects.

pages.text: Crossbill I am a crossbill. My beak is crossed like an X, which helps me to pull the seeds out of a pinecone. Pinecones grow on trees called conifers, but conifers don’t produce good pinecones every year. I travel all over to find pinecones instead of living in one place.
pages.brief: A crossbill uses its crossed, X-shaped beak to pull seeds out of a pinecone. It travels all over to find pinecones on conifer trees instead of living in one place, because conifers do not produce good pinecones every year.

pages.text: Rhinoceros Hornbill I am a rhinoceros hornbill. I have a horn on the top of my beak that I use to knock down fruit. I also use my horn to fight and sometimes to attract a mate. I bring food to my mate when she sits on our eggs. If you think my horn looks weird, you should see my eyelashes! I am one of the few birds that have them.
pages.brief: A rhinoceros hornbill has a horn on top of its beak. It uses the horn to knock down fruit, to fight, and sometimes to attract a mate. It brings food to its mate while she sits on their eggs, and it has unusual eyelashes.

pages.text: Huia We are huias (HOO-yuhs). We lived in New Zealand until we became extinct. “I am the male. My beak is thick and strong.” “I am the female. My beak is thin and curved.” Our beaks are so different that for a long time, people thought we were completely different types of birds.
pages.brief: A male and a female huia are shown in New Zealand. The male has a thick, strong beak; the female has a thin, curved beak. These birds are extinct. Their beaks are so different that people once thought they were completely different types of birds.

pages.text: Sword-Billed Hummingbird I am a sword-billed hummingbird. I am a very small bird with a very long beak. I’m the only bird with a bill that is longer than my body! I use my long beak and even longer tongue to get nectar from tube- shaped flowers. I can stick my tongue out and pull it back in again about 13 times per second!
pages.brief: A tiny sword-billed hummingbird has a bill longer than its whole body. It reaches into tube-shaped flowers with its long beak and even longer tongue to get nectar. It can stick its tongue out and pull it back in about 13 times per second.

pages.text: Brown Pelican I am a brown pelican. I have a pouch of skin under my beak that can hold a lot of fish. I hunt in the ocean, diving down from the air. I sometimes steal fish from other birds, but they steal from me, too. Gulls even sit on my head and back while they take fish right out of my pouch!
pages.brief: A brown pelican has a pouch of skin under its beak that can hold a lot of fish. It hunts in the ocean by diving down from the air. Gulls sit on its head and back while taking fish right out of its pouch.

pages.text: Shoebill Stork I am a shoebill stork. My beak is shaped like a shoe with a hook on the end that helps me eat fish. Sometimes, I’ll eat frogs and even small crocodiles. I hunt fish by waiting for one to swim by and then falling onto it with my mouth open.
pages.brief: A shoebill stork has a beak shaped like a shoe with a hook on the end. It uses it to eat fish, and sometimes frogs and even small crocodiles. It hunts by waiting for a fish to swim by, then falling onto it with its mouth open.

pages.text: Spoonbill I am a spoonbill. I have a long beak that flattens out at the end like a spoon. Because I am white and pink, people sometimes think I’m a flamingo. To find food, I sweep my beak back and forth in the mud and shallow water. I like to eat frogs, shellfish, seaweed, and small fish.
pages.brief: A spoonbill has a long beak that flattens out at the end like a spoon. Because it is white and pink, people sometimes mistake it for a flamingo. It sweeps its beak back and forth in mud and shallow water to find frogs, shellfish, seaweed, and small fish.

pages.text: Toucan I am a toucan. My huge and colorful beak is actually very light because it’s full of air pockets. I eat fruit, seeds, insects, and eggs. My beak helps me to reach fruit while I sit in rainforest trees. I have two claws that point forward and two that point backward to help me hold onto branches.
pages.brief: A toucan sits in rainforest trees and reaches fruit with its huge, colorful beak. The beak is very light because it is full of air pockets. The bird eats fruit, seeds, insects, and eggs, and its two forward and two backward claws help it hold onto branches.

pages.text: Many of us have weird beaks. Sometimes they help us to catch or eat food. Sometimes they just look wild!
pages.brief: A group of birds with weird beaks is shown together. Some of their strange beaks help them catch or eat food, while other beaks simply look wild. Each bird displays its own unusual beak shape.

books.art_why: Elephants are real animals that exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: The Largest Land Animal Did you know that elephants are the largest land animals in the world? I saw an amazing picture of a mother elephant with her baby. I wanted to learn more about elephants, so I checked out a book from the library. I learned many unusual facts about elephants that I can share with you.
pages.brief: A child in a library looks at an amazing photo of a mother elephant standing beside her baby. The child holds a library book about elephants, eager to learn unusual facts and share them with readers.

pages.text: Elephant Bodies If you’ve ever seen an elephant in a zoo, you know they are huge. An adult male can weigh as much as six cars. I definitely don’t want an elephant to sit on me! Elephants have heavy gray bodies, thick legs, wrinkled skin, and floppy ears. Many elephants also have a pair of tusks, which are long, pointed teeth. Elephants use their tusks to peel the minerals. Do You Know?

pages.text: One really interesting part of an elephant is its long trunk. An elephant’s trunk is its nose and upper lip joined together into a special shape. An elephant can use its trunk like a hand to pick up food or other objects. The trunk works like a hose when an elephant drinks water or gives itself a shower. A trunk can even Do You Know? work like a snorkel, helping an elephant breathe underwater.

pages.text: Elephant Families Elephants live in families of four to ten females and their young. The females, called cows, are all aunts, sisters, and daughters. A wise old female called the matriarch (MAY-tree-ark) is the leader of the family. She helps her family find food and water. She also keeps the family together and helps everyone stay safe.

pages.text: Male elephants stay with their mothers until they are about 11 years old—teenagers, in elephant years. Then they go to live with other males. Adult males, called bulls, often live alone except when they mate with females. Sometimes bulls use their tusks to fight each other for a female.

pages.text: Baby elephants, called calves, are incredibly cute! When a calf is born, everyone in the family strokes it with his or her trunk to welcome it. All the adults help care for the calves. If a calf gets stuck in the mud at a water hole, everyone helps pull it Do You Know? out. If a lion is near, the adults stand in a circle around all the calves to protect them.
pages.brief: A newborn elephant calf stands with its family at a water hole; adults gently stroke it with their trunks. When a calf is stuck in mud, family members pull it out. Nearby, adults form a protective circle around calves as a lion watches.

pages.text: Food and Water Elephants are herbivores (UR-beh- vores), or plant eaters, and they like many kinds of food. They eat grass, leaves, bark, branches, fruit, flowers, and seeds. Elephants are always on the for food and water. They eat so much that they can’t stay in one place for very long. When they leave an area, the plants have time to grow back.
pages.brief: Elephants, plant-eating herbivores, feed on grass, leaves, bark, branches, fruit, flowers and seeds. They are always on the move searching for food and water, eating so much that they cannot stay in one place long; then plants can grow back.

pages.text: Sometimes three or more families of elephants join together to form a herd. A herd may travel together to look for food and water. Elephants often walk in single file with each family following its matriarch. They follow the same routes year after year as they move from place to place.
pages.brief: Three or more elephant families form a herd and travel together looking for food and water. They walk in single file, each family following its matriarch along the same routes year after year across the land.

pages.text: Elephants need to drink water, just like people. Because they live in hot places, they also need water to cool off. Elephants like to give themselves showers. They also like to roll in mud or cover with dust. Elephant skin tough, but it’s sensitive. Mud and dust and the Sun’s heat.
pages.brief: Elephants drink water and use it to cool off in hot places. Some give themselves showers, roll in mud or cover themselves with dust. Their skin is tough but sensitive as they deal with mud, dust and the sun's heat.

pages.text: Keeping Elephants Alive I was sad to learn that both kinds of elephants are endangered. Even though it is against the law, people kill elephants for their tusks. The tusks are made of ivory, which people use to make jewelry and pieces of art. People also change a lot of wild land into farms, which leaves some elephants with no place to live.
pages.brief: An African elephant and an Asian elephant stand near wild land being changed into farmland. Carved ivory jewelry and pieces of art lie nearby, showing that people kill elephants for tusks; both kinds are endangered and losing places to live.

pages.text: Many people around the world are trying to save elephants. Some countries have created special parks to protect elephants. Hunters are less likely to kill elephants that live in the parks than ones that live in the wild. Elephants are amazing animals. I hope people can help these gentle giants stay alive for a very long time.
pages.brief: Elephants roam safely inside a special park created to protect them. People around the world work to save these gentle giants, and elephants in parks are less likely to be killed by hunters than those in the wild.

books.title: Bedbugs Bite!
books.art_why: Bedbugs, homes, dogs and bites are real today and can be photographed accurately.

pages.text: Introduction Good night. Sleep tight. Don’t let the bedbugs bite! These words were just an old rhyme a few years ago. Bedbugs (or “bed bugs”) were hard to find. But today these words are good advice. Bedbugs have returned. These little pests are causing big problems in cities all over the world.
pages.brief: A small brown bedbug crawls along the seam of a white mattress in a dim bedroom at night. A sleeping person’s blanket is nearby. Through a window, city apartment buildings glow, showing that bedbugs are causing problems in cities again.

pages.text: What Are Bedbugs? Bedbugs are brown, crawling insects that grow to be about the size of apple seeds. They hide in tight spaces during the day and are active at night. As their name suggests, bedbugs often live in people’s beds. They might be hiding under your mattress. Bedbugs bite people or other animals to drink their blood.
pages.brief: A close-up of a brown bedbug, about the size of an apple seed, crawling out of a tight mattress seam in a bedroom at night. Another bedbug hides in a narrow crack nearby. A person’s arm rests on the sheet, showing where the insect bites to drink blood.

pages.text: Bedbugs are not attracted to dirt or garbage. They don’t care if their hiding spots are fancy or plain. People who keep their homes clean can get them. People with a lot of money or a little money can get them. Even movie stars get bedbugs!
pages.brief: Bedbugs hide in a clean, fancy bedroom and in a simple, plain bedroom, showing they do not care about dirt or money. One bedbug crawls near a tidy bed; another hides by a plain wall. A glamorous movie star stands in a fancy room, also bothered by bedbugs.

pages.text: Unlike mosquitoes, which fly around to find their meals, bedbugs like the easy life. They bite when a person is quiet and still. Their victims may be sleeping in bed or sitting quietly, watching TV.
pages.brief: A bedbug crawls across a bedsheet toward a sleeping person, while a mosquito flies in the background for contrast. In another room, a person sits quietly on a sofa watching television, and a bedbug moves close to an uncovered arm.

pages.text: Bedbug Life Cycle It doesn’t take very long for a few bedbugs to become a lot of bedbugs. A female bedbug can lay more than two hundred eggs in her lifetime. The eggs hatch in six to ten days. When a bedbug eats, its body swells up. As it digests its food, its body shrinks. As a bedbug grows up, its outer skin becomes too tight for its body. When this happens, the bug molts, or sheds, its outer skin. A bedbug molts five times before it is an adult. A developing bedbug can go for months without eating. An adult bedbug can go for a year without food. But if a bedbug lives near people, it will eat every day.
pages.brief: A female bedbug lays a cluster of tiny eggs near a mattress seam. Young bedbugs hatch, feed, swell, and shrink as they digest. One bedbug sheds its tight outer skin. The sequence shows a young bedbug growing through five molts toward adulthood, with an adult bedbug hiding nearby.

pages.text: Bedbug Life Cycle.
pages.brief: A close-up photo sequence of bedbug eggs, a small young bedbug, a shed outer skin, and a full-grown adult bedbug on a plain white surface. The young bug is shown at different sizes, making clear how it grows and molts before becoming an adult.

pages.text: World Travelers Bedbugs can’t fly. They only walk as fast as ladybugs. But these little critters travel all over the world. How do they do it? They sneak rides with people who are traveling.
pages.brief: A bedbug walks slowly across a folded jacket inside an open suitcase near waiting travelers. Nearby, a ladybug walks on a leaf for a speed comparison. People with rolling luggage move past, showing how bedbugs ride with travelers to reach places around the world.

pages.text: A suitcase or moving box makes a good hiding spot for a bedbug. If a family brings that suitcase to a hotel, the bugs may crawl out. Some of the bedbugs might find hiding spots in the hotel. Some might hide in another person’s suitcase and go home with them. Once they get to a new home, bedbugs travel from room to room by squeezing through tiny cracks in the walls or floors.
pages.brief: A family sets a suitcase down in a hotel room. Brown bedbugs crawl out from the suitcase seam and hide in a mattress and a wall crack. Another traveler’s suitcase sits nearby. In a home, bedbugs squeeze through a tiny crack between the wall and floor to reach another room.

pages.text: Getting Rid of Bedbugs It’s easy to spot bedbug bites. Many people get red, itchy bumps on their skin when they are bitten. But it’s not as easy to spot the bedbugs. They can hide in tiny places and only come out when it’s dark. But there are ways to find them.
pages.brief: A close-up of a person’s arm with red, itchy bumps from bedbug bites. In a dim bedroom, a bedbug hides in a tiny mattress fold and stays out of sight. A person leans close to the bed, looking carefully for the pests in the dark.

pages.text: Bedbugs often leave clues that they are around. If you look closely, you may find shed skin and dark spots of dried excrement, or poop, near their hiding areas. But the best way to find them is to hire a special dog. Some dogs are trained to smell bedbugs. They sniff all over homes or hotel rooms. When they smell bedbugs, they place a paw on the spot. Once the bugs are discovered, people can get rid of them with steam or chemicals.
pages.brief: A trained dog sniffs all over a hotel room, then places a paw on a mattress seam. Near the bed, shed bedbug skins and dark dried spots show where the insects hide. Later, steam and chemical spray are used to get rid of the bedbugs.

pages.text: Conclusion Bedbugs are becoming common again in cities around the world. They are biting more people. Their bites don’t hurt, and they usually don’t spread germs or disease. But it’s still not nice to get them; they can itch—a lot. Things You Can Do: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5.
pages.brief: A nighttime city scene shows lit apartment windows, with bedbugs hiding in beds inside several homes. A person sits on a bed, scratching red, itchy bites on an arm. The bites look harmless and do not show signs of serious disease, but the person is clearly uncomfortable.

pages.text: If you do get bedbug bites, try to not scratch them. They can get infected if they are scratched open. And remember, you are not alone. People all over the world get bedbug bites. That’s why for years people have said, “Good night. Sleep tight. Don’t let the bedbugs bite!”
pages.brief: A child sits on a bed with red bedbug bites on an arm and keeps their hands away from the itchy spots, trying not to scratch. In a soft nighttime scene, people in different homes around the world sleep under blankets, showing that bedbug bites happen everywhere.

books.title: Watching Earth From Space
books.art_why: Real satellites, storms, pollution, and landscapes exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Introduction The world around you has hills, trees, and buildings. Stand on the sidewalk. You will only see what is happening on your street. That is your normal view. Now imagine looking down at your town from space. You would have a much wider view. From space, you could see your entire country!
pages.brief: A child stands on a sidewalk on a street with hills, trees, and buildings around, looking down the street. Above, a wide view from space shows the whole town and the entire country spread out below.

pages.text: Scientists can study Earth from space. They use cameras on satellites that circle the Earth. The International Space Station is one satellite that has cameras.
pages.brief: Several satellites with cameras circle Earth high above, including the International Space Station. Below, scientists in a control room study Earth, watching the satellite pictures on screens as the cameras record the planet from space.

pages.text: Pictures made by these cameras show changes that happen to Earth over time. These pictures record how the land changes. They show problems like pollution and climate changes.
pages.brief: A satellite above Earth sends back camera pictures of the same land over time. The pictures show the land changing, with areas of pollution and signs of climate change visible clearly across the landscape below.

pages.text: Weather Satellites Watch Storms Large storms can cause great damage. A storm warning system lets people know a dangerous storm is coming. However, not all areas have warning systems. People might not have time to escape a storm’s path. Satellite pictures help scientists predict where a storm will go. Then they can tell people to leave that area.
pages.brief: A huge storm swirls over land and sea, seen from a weather satellite above. Scientists track the storm’s path on screens. Below, people leave a town in the storm’s path, while dark clouds gather overhead.

pages.text: Keeping Watch on Pollution Pictures from space can show where air or water is being polluted. For example, they can show where an oil spill is spreading. This information helps people who live nearby. It also helps with cleanup efforts. Satellite pictures record how long it takes for the environment to recover.
pages.brief: A satellite view shows an oil spill spreading across the ocean. Nearby, cleanup boats work on the water, and people who live along the coast watch. The pictures record how long the environment takes to recover.

pages.text: Air pollution can affect the health of large groups of people. Satellite pictures show where the dirty air starts. The pictures also show where the dirty air goes. For example, some overcrowded cities in China have very dirty air. There are many causes, such as burning coal for power. Pictures show the coal pollution drifting to other countries.
pages.brief: A satellite view shows an overcrowded city in China under a thick layer of dirty air. Coal-burning power plants release smoke, and the hazy pollution drifts from the city across the land toward other countries.

pages.text: Watching Changes to the Land Pictures from space show changes to land areas. For example, they show deforestation, or the loss of forests. They also show where land has worn away because of wind or water. Deforestation is a world problem. Trees help keep our air clean. They are home to wildlife. Photos from space show large forest areas that have been cut down or burned.
pages.brief: A satellite view shows a large forest area where trees have been cut down or burned, leaving bare ground. In the remaining forest, trees stand tall, home to wildlife and helping keep the air clean.

pages.text: Deforestation is also a cause of land wearing away. That is because tree roots help to hold soil in place. Without tree roots, the soil slides away. Serious land loss has happened on the island of Madagascar. Entire forests have been cut down. People remove trees to use them or make space for new farmland. Photos show large amounts of soil being washed away and lost.
pages.brief: On Madagascar, a satellite view shows entire forests cut down. People remove trees for wood and farmland. Without tree roots to hold it, soil slides away, and large amounts of soil wash away and are lost.

pages.text: Watching Climate Change Effects Scientists say people are causing a lot of the changes in Earth’s climate. When we burn oil, coal, and natural gas we create gas in the air. This type of gas traps more heat than usual above Earth. Pictures from space show the effects of Earth becoming warmer. For example, they show where ice is melting or breaking apart.
pages.brief: A satellite view of Earth shows ice melting and breaking apart. Below, power plants and vehicles burn oil, coal, and natural gas, sending gas into the air that traps more heat than usual above the planet.

pages.text: Another result of Earth becoming warmer is the spread of deserts. Satellite pictures show where land is too dry. People can’t grow food or feed animals there. N Thinking Critically.
pages.brief: A satellite view shows land turning too dry as deserts spread. The dry ground stretches out, and people cannot grow food or feed animals there. The desert spreads across the land under the hot sun.

pages.text: Conclusion For most of history, people could see a small part of the world. They viewed everything at eye level. Even people who traveled could only see what was right in front of them.
pages.brief: A person stands at eye level on a road, seeing only the small part of the world right in front of them. Travelers on the road see only what is directly ahead, not the wider world beyond.

pages.text: Today we can easily watch and track large areas of Earth. Pictures from satellite cameras tell us about Earth’s changes. They help us understand how changes happening far away might affect us. What we do with that knowledge may decide the future of our planet.
pages.brief: People look at satellite pictures on screens, tracking large areas of Earth. A satellite above sends back views of changes far away. The people use this knowledge to understand how those changes might affect them and the planet’s future.

books.title: Beyond the Five Senses
books.art_why: Real animals, people and natural settings can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Animals use senses to find food and stay out of danger. Our senses tell us what is happening with our bodies and in the world around us. You probably know about the five basic senses: hearing, sight, smell, touch, and taste. Did you know that animals can also have many other senses? Some of these senses are common to most animals. Others are rare and amazing.
pages.brief: A child outdoors in a park touches a leaf, listens to a bird and looks at a flower, showing sight, hearing, touch, smell and taste. Around them, a rabbit, bird and fox use their senses to find food and avoid danger. Some animals nearby show surprising extra senses.

pages.text: Body-Position Sense Without looking, do you know where your left foot is right now? You can answer this question because your brain senses where your body parts are. Without this sense, an animal would not be able to move and do interesting things with its body.
pages.brief: A child stands with eyes closed, one foot lifted slightly, aware of where their left foot is without looking. A cutaway view shows the brain sensing the position of legs, arms and feet. The child’s body is ready to move because it knows where each part is.

pages.text: Pain Sense Pain might seem as though it’s part of the sense of touch, but it isn’t. People and other animals can feel pain even when nothing is touching them. Pain helps us by letting us know that we’ve been hurt. It can also warn us to stop or change what we are doing before we get hurt.
pages.brief: A child holds a scraped knee and winces, feeling pain even though nothing is touching the scrape. Nearby, a dog stops and limps, warned by pain to change what it is doing. Pain signals that a body has been hurt and can help prevent further injury.

pages.text: Sense of Balance Humans and many other animals have tubes inside their ears that give them a sense of balance. Other senses, such as sight and knowing where your body parts are, make balancing easier. That is why balancing is more difficult when your eyes are closed or your leg is “asleep.”
pages.brief: A child stands on one leg with eyes closed, wobbling because balance is harder without sight. Inside the ear, tubes help give a sense of balance. The child uses sight and body-position sense to steady themselves, showing why balancing is easier with eyes open.

pages.text: Temperature Sense Sensing hot and cold is important for many animals. Some bats and snakes have special heat sensors that can help them find prey. A rattlesnake can “feel” the heat of a mouse’s body from over a foot away.
pages.brief: A rattlesnake waits on the ground and senses the body heat of a small mouse more than a foot away. A bat flies overhead with special heat sensors of its own. These sensors help the animals find prey even when the prey is hidden.

pages.text: Time Sense Scientists think humans have the best sense of time, but there’s a chance that other animals sense it, too. For example, dogs and cats sometimes seem to sense when it’s time for their owners to come home.
pages.brief: A dog waits by the door and a cat sits by a window, both seeming to sense when their owner will come home. The owner is away, and the animals expect their return. Scientists think humans have the best sense of time, but dogs and cats may sense it too.

pages.text: Using Sounds to “See” Some animals use sounds to “see” the things around them, even deep underwater or in the dark. By making sounds and listening to echoes, these animals can tell where things are. Some bats, dolphins, whales, and birds have this special sense.
pages.brief: A bat flies through a dark cave, making sounds and listening to echoes to find where things are. A dolphin swims deep underwater and uses echoes to sense the fish around it. Some whales and birds also use sounds to “see” in the dark.

pages.text: Bonus-Color Vision Did you know that nature has more colors than the human eye can see? Some birds and insects can see those extra colors. Seeing extra colors helps these animals find food or attract mates.
pages.brief: A bird perches near bright flowers and sees extra colors beyond the human rainbow, helping it find food. A bee flies toward colorful petals, using its color vision to find food. Both animals can see colors that the human eye cannot.

pages.text: Whisker Sense Whiskers on animals aren’t just cute. Whiskers help animals to sense movement in the air or water around them. Whiskers can also help animals squeeze through small spaces or catch other animals with their mouths.
pages.brief: An animal squeezes through a narrow gap, using its whiskers to sense the space around its face. Another animal swims in water and feels movement with its whiskers. Whiskers help animals sense movement in air or water and catch prey with their mouths.

pages.text: Electric-Field Sense Every animal’s body gives off a weak electric field. Humans and most other animals can’t sense these fields, but some animals that live in water can. Some sharks can find fish hiding in the sand on the ocean floor just by using this sense.
pages.brief: A shark swims above the sandy ocean floor and senses the weak electric field of a fish hiding in the sand. The fish is buried and out of sight, but the shark can find it using this special sense. Humans and most animals cannot sense electric fields.

pages.text: Magnetic-Field Sense The needle in a compass always points north because of Earth’s magnetic field. Some animals have a kind of natural compass built into their bodies. These animals can always “feel” which way is north, so they can travel long distances without getting lost.
pages.brief: An animal travels across a wide landscape, feeling Earth’s magnetic field like a natural compass built into its body. It knows which way is north and can go a long distance without getting lost. A compass needle points north nearby, showing the same magnetic field.

pages.text: Conclusion There are many senses beyond hearing, sight, smell, touch, and taste. As you explore the world, think about the extra senses that animals, including you, use every day.
pages.brief: A child explores outdoors, watching animals and noticing the many senses beyond hearing, sight, smell, touch and taste. Around the child, animals use extra senses in their own surroundings. The child thinks about how animals, including people, use these senses every day.

books.title: What Lives in This Hole?
books.art_why: Real animals, real burrows and a real child photographer — all things that exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Animal Burrows I found a big hole in the ground two months ago. I thought it might be an animal’s burrow. I took a picture with my phone to show my teacher.
pages.brief: A young child stands outdoors in a grassy field, holding up a phone to photograph a large dark hole in the ground. Loose soil is piled at the hole's edge. The child leans forward, curious, with trees and open ground behind.

pages.text: She helped me find out what lives in the hole. Now I study the burrow of a different animal every week. Then I write about it on our class blog. Check out what I’ve learned!
pages.brief: The child sits at a classroom computer with a teacher leaning in to help, both looking at the screen together. A notebook and pencil lie open nearby. The child is writing up a burrow, ready to share the findings on the class blog.

pages.text: Do You Know? Staying Cool A desert tortoise lives in this hole! This animal lives in a desert. It digs a burrow to get away from the heat. It spends most of its life in the burrow.
pages.brief: A desert tortoise rests deep inside a sandy burrow, its shell half in shadow. Outside, dry desert ground, rocks and sparse plants stretch under hot sun. The tortoise's sturdy front legs show it has been digging into the cool earth.

pages.text: Wowser! Keeping Eggs Safe A huge spider lives in this hole! It lives in a deep burrow. A female lays about fifty eggs in a little bag. She takes the bag with her if she leaves to hunt.
pages.brief: A large spider sits in a deep, dark burrow, a small silken egg bag held close. Around her the burrow walls are packed earth. Her long legs spread wide as she guards the bag holding about fifty eggs.

pages.text: Making a Nest This hole belongs to puffins! These birds spend most of their life at sea. They use their strong wings and webbed feet to fly and swim. Puffins swim much better than they fly.
pages.brief: Puffins float on the open sea, black and white with bright beaks, paddling and diving on webbed feet. One bird beats its strong wings low over the water. Waves rise around them in the wide ocean.

pages.text: Wowser! Puffins use a burrow as a nest. They dig the burrow on a high cliff near water. Both parents care for the egg and then the chick.
pages.brief: On a high cliff above the water, two puffins stand at the entrance of a dug burrow. One parent sits close over a single egg, and then a fluffy chick. Sea stretches below the cliff edge, grass and soil around the nest hole.

pages.text: Living in the Dark Naked mole rats live in this hole! They spend their whole lives in the dark. They dig tunnels to find roots and other plant parts to eat.
pages.brief: In total darkness underground, naked mole rats with pink wrinkled skin and big front teeth tunnel through soil. One gnaws at a plant root while others crowd the narrow passage. No light reaches them in their deep, dark home.

pages.text: Naked mole rats work together to build tunnels. One animal digs through soil at the front. Several others sweep dirt toward the back. An animal at the back kicks the dirt out of the tunnel.
pages.brief: A line of naked mole rats works inside a tunnel. At the front, one digs through soil with its teeth. Behind it, several sweep loose dirt backward with their feet, and the last animal kicks the dirt out of the tunnel opening.

pages.text: Wowser! Hiding and Laying Eggs A big salamander lives in this underwater hole! It lives in rivers and streams. It hides in a burrow or under rocks during the day. It comes out to hunt at night.
pages.brief: A big salamander hides in an underwater burrow in a stream, its spotted body pressed against the mud. Rocks and flowing water surround it. The dim water shows it stays hidden by day and comes out to hunt at night.

pages.text: In late summer, males and females gather at burrows. A female lays up to five hundred eggs there. A male watches the eggs to make sure fish don’t eat them.
pages.brief: In late summer, several big salamanders gather at burrows in a stream bed. A female lays a cluster of eggs, up to five hundred, in the water. A male hovers over the eggs, watching as fish swim nearby.

pages.text: Wowser! Taking a Nap A wombat lives in this hole! This animal digs a burrow with its huge claws. It sleeps in its burrow during the day. At night, it comes out to find plants to eat.
pages.brief: A wombat with thick fur and huge claws digs into the earth, soil scattering behind it. Inside the burrow it curls up asleep during the day. At night it stands outside, feeding on plants and grass.

pages.text: More to Come I’m going to study more animals that live in holes. Next, I will write about rabbits, snakes, and ants. It’s so fun to learn about animals!
pages.brief: The child sits outdoors with a notebook, looking at a hole in the ground and planning ahead. Nearby are a rabbit, a snake and ants, the next animals to study. The child smiles, eager to learn more.

books.title: Asthma
books.art_why: Real-world health topic with people and medical equipment; no historical event or named-person biography.

pages.text: What Is Asthma? Asthma is a disease that makes it difficult for a person to breathe. When people breathe, air makes its way through the nose or mouth to the lungs. Air moves in and out of the lungs through special tubes.
pages.brief: A person breathes in through the nose and mouth, while a medical model of the body shows air traveling down to the lungs. The lungs and special tubes are visible as air moves in and out.

pages.text: These tubes swell and become narrow during an asthma attack. Because of this, less air moves into and out of the lungs. People with asthma might wheeze or cough. Their chest might feel tight. They may have a hard time breathing. A bad asthma attack can last for days or even cause death.
pages.brief: A child with asthma sits with a hand on a tight chest, coughing and struggling to breathe. Inside the body, the special tubes look swollen and narrow, so less air moves into and out of the lungs.

pages.text: People with Asthma About 235 million children and adults around the world have asthma. Asthma can show up in a person at any age. About one child out of every ten in the United States has asthma. About half of these children will see their asthma get better as they grow older. However, their symptoms often return when they become older adults. One adult in twelve has asthma. Each year, more people in the United States and around the world get asthma.
pages.brief: A large group of children and adults of different ages from around the world stands together in one wide scene. Some are young children and some are older adults, representing the many people who have asthma.

pages.text: Children Under Age 15 with Asthma in the United States: 2009 Doctors do not know how people get asthma. They do know that it cannot be passed from one person to another like a cold. However, the disease often runs in families. If both parents have asthma, their children are more likely to have it. People who are around cigarette smoke are also more likely to develop asthma.
pages.brief: Several children under age fifteen stand together in a United States setting. Two parents stand close to their child, and cigarette smoke drifts near another person nearby; the scene focuses on families and smoke exposure.

pages.text: The Causes of Attacks Many things can cause asthma attacks. These triggers are different from person to person. Dust, animals, pollen, or mold can cause an attack for many people. Cigarette smoke, fumes from cars, and other strong smells are also common triggers. Coming down with a cold or the flu can often bring on an attack as well. Exercise can cause an asthma attack in some people.
pages.brief: A person with asthma stands in a room and outdoors near common triggers: dust, an animal, pollen, mold, cigarette smoke, car fumes, and a strong smell. Another person with a cold or flu and someone exercising are nearby.

pages.text: Keeping Asthma Under Control Most people with asthma learn to control the disease. They often start by meeting with their doctor to create an action plan. Each person’s action plan is a little different. It can include a person’s triggers and how to avoid them. It can also include the kinds of medicines a person uses and how to use them correctly.
pages.brief: A person with asthma sits with a doctor in a clinic, and together they create an action plan. The plan includes the person’s triggers, ways to avoid them, and the medicines the person uses correctly.

pages.text: People use different medicines to control asthma. Some people take pills every day. Others may take pills only when they feel the symptoms of asthma. Many people use inhalers. These devices spray a mist of medicine that is breathed in. Inhalers may be used daily or only when a person has an asthma attack.
pages.brief: A person with asthma takes a pill with water and then uses an inhaler. The inhaler sprays a mist of medicine that the person breathes in, while another person takes a pill only when symptoms appear.

pages.text: Do You Know?
pages.brief: A curious child in a bright room raises a hand as if asking a question, and an adult listens nearby. The child looks thoughtful, and the scene suggests a moment for learning more about asthma.

pages.text: Another important part of keeping asthma under control is staying healthy. Exercise, a healthy diet, and plenty of sleep can help keep asthma under control.
pages.brief: A child with asthma exercises, eats a healthy meal, and sleeps. The child moves actively outdoors, sits at a table with healthy food, and rests in bed with plenty of sleep, showing habits that help keep asthma under control.

pages.text: Living with Asthma People with asthma can do anything that anyone else can. Many famous athletes have asthma. Jerome “The Bus” Bettis was fourteen when doctors told him he had asthma. It did not stop him from becoming a Super Bowl champion.
pages.brief: Jerome “The Bus” Bettis stands in a football stadium as a Super Bowl champion. He was fourteen when doctors told him he had asthma, and the scene shows him strong and active on the field.

pages.text: Amy Van Dyken was an Olympic swimmer for the United States. She has asthma and won six gold medals. When she was a child, her doctor said that she should start swimming to make her lungs stronger.
pages.brief: Amy Van Dyken swims in a pool as an Olympic swimmer for the United States. As a child, her doctor told her to start swimming to make her lungs stronger, and she later won six gold medals.

pages.text: People with asthma have climbed the tallest mountains. They have explored the deep waters of the ocean. They have led countries and made discoveries that have changed the world. With an action plan and a healthy lifestyle, asthma doesn’t have to slow anyone down.
pages.brief: A group of people with asthma are shown in bold settings: one climbs a tall mountain, one explores deep ocean water, one leads a country, and one makes a discovery. With an action plan and healthy lifestyle, they are not slowed down.

books.title: Awesome Ants
books.art_why: Keyword check selects drawing, which suits clear ant anatomy and the dinosaur-era view.

pages.text: A Little History You’ve seen them marching through grass and across sidewalks. You may have even seen them crawling over your kitchen counter. We’re talking about ants—tiny, strong, awesome ants.
pages.brief: Tiny strong ants march through grass and across a sidewalk. Several crawl over a kitchen counter, their small bodies moving in a line as they explore. The scene shows the ants close enough to see their busy movement and strength.

pages.text: Ants are about 100 million years old. They were crawling around under the dinosaurs! Between then and now, they’ve changed a lot. Today, over 10,000 species of ants live on every continent except Antarctica. They have been able to survive so long because of their bodies and how they live.
pages.brief: Ancient ants crawl beneath huge dinosaurs. Later, modern ants of many kinds spread across every continent except Antarctica. The picture contrasts the distant past with today, showing how ants changed and survived because of their bodies and how they live.

pages.text: Body Parts Like all insects, ants have six legs and three body parts. The back part of their body is the abdomen. This part holds the heart and stomachs. Some ants have stingers that they use to protect themselves. Their three pairs of legs attach to the middle part, called the thorax. Each leg has little hooks that allow ants to climb almost anything. Ants can even hear with their legs by feeling vibrations through the ground.
pages.brief: A close view of an ant shows six legs and three body parts. The abdomen holds the heart and stomachs, and a stinger protects it. Three pairs of legs attach to the thorax, each leg with little hooks for climbing. Vibrations pass through the ground as the ant hears with its legs.

pages.text: The head contains the brain, two eyes, antennae, and jaws. The jaws open and close like scissors. They are used for cutting and carrying things. Ants can lift more than twenty times their own weight. Ants also have other mouthparts for chewing food and drinking.
pages.brief: An ant’s head fills the view, with its brain, two eyes, antennae, and scissor-like jaws. The jaws cut and carry a load. The ant lifts something more than twenty times its own weight. Other mouthparts chew food and drink, showing the head’s many uses.

pages.text: The two eyes are each made up of many smaller eyes. Even though ants have so many eyes, they can’t see very well. Instead, they use their antennae to get around. The antennae are like all-in-one sense machines. Ants use them to taste, smell, hear, and communicate with other ants through touching. The long, thin antennae are always moving around.
pages.brief: The ant’s two eyes are made of many smaller eyes, yet it cannot see very well. Long, thin antennae move constantly as all-in-one sense machines. The ant uses them to taste, smell, hear, and touch another ant, communicating through the contact.

pages.text: Let’s Talk Ants communicate with each other in three ways: touch, sound, and smell. Ants touch each other with their antennae in different ways to send different messages. They can also make noises to communicate by rubbing their legs together or on their bodies.
pages.brief: Ants communicate in three ways: touch, sound, and smell. One ant touches another with its antennae, sending a message. Another rubs its legs together or on its body to make noises. The scene shows ants close together, using touch and sound.

pages.text: The main way ants communicate is by smell. They release chemicals that other ants can smell long after the first ant is gone. Different smells send different messages. For example, a crushed ant releases chemicals that attract other ants. The chemicals also make the other ants attack anything nearby that might be a danger. An ant that has found food will lay down a trail of chemicals for other ants to follow. The trail allows them to find the food and return to the colony.
pages.brief: The main way ants communicate is by smell. An ant that finds food lays a chemical trail for others to follow back to the colony. A crushed ant releases chemicals that attract other ants, making them attack anything nearby that might be a danger.

pages.text: One Big, Happy Family Ant colonies with activity. Usually built they have many which all have different uses. Some rooms are used to care for the young. Colonies even have rooms for ants to relax in.
pages.brief: Inside an ant colony, many rooms are busy with activity. The rooms have different uses. Some rooms are used to care for the young, while other rooms are places for ants to relax. The nest shows ants working and resting in its many spaces.

pages.text: Within the colony, every ant has a job. Worker ants and soldier ants find food and protect the nest. These are usually the ants you see above the ground. Other ants build the nest, take care of the young, and do other jobs. All these ants are female, but What About only one is allowed the Boys? to lay eggs: the queen. In other words, all the ants in a colony are related.
pages.brief: Worker ants and soldier ants find food and protect the nest above the ground. Other ants build the nest and care for the young inside. Every ant has a job. All are female, but only the queen lays eggs, and all the ants in the colony are related.

pages.text: The Queen The queen is the leader of the colony. The largest of all the ants, queens are egg-laying machines. Some queens can lay thousands of eggs every day. They can also live longer than most other insects— over twenty-five years. I Can Fly!
pages.brief: The queen is the largest ant and the leader of the colony. She is an egg-laying machine, laying thousands of eggs every day. Some queens live over twenty-five years, longer than most other insects. The winged queen spreads her wings, showing that she can fly.

pages.text: Let’s Go Floating Yep, Ants Are Awesome Ants may be small, but they can do awesome things. Thousands or millions of ants working together can build bridges or float across rivers. They can overpower animals hundreds of times their own size for food.
pages.brief: Thousands or millions of ants work together. They link together to build bridges and float across a river. The tiny ants also overpower animals hundreds of times their own size to get food. Their small bodies show awesome strength when they act as one group.

pages.text: So the next time you come across a trail of ants, stop and watch or, better yet, follow them. When you see what these little gals are capable of, you’ll understand just how awesome they are.
pages.brief: A trail of ants crosses the ground. The small female ants work together, and the scene invites a close look or a follow along the trail. Watching what these little ants are capable of reveals just how awesome they are.

books.title: Roadside Oddities
books.art_why: The roadside attractions are real places that exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: What Is The Thing? Giant signs at the side of the road ask, “The Thing? What is it?” Roadside attractions such as The Thing are odd and wonderful. They ask people to stop and check them out.
pages.brief: At the side of a highway, giant signs for a roadside attraction called The Thing stand tall and strange. Curious travelers slow down and stop to check out the odd, wonderful attraction, wondering what it is.

pages.text: World’s Largest Baseball Bat The world’s largest baseball bat is taller than the five- story building it stands beside. It weighs as much as three school buses.
pages.brief: A colossal baseball bat stands upright beside a five-story building, towering far above the roof. The giant roadside bat is shown at its enormous scale; it looks taller than the building and as heavy as three school buses.

pages.text: The Corn Palace The Corn Palace is decorated with grasses and corn of different colors. The Corn Palace is also the world’s largest bird feeder. When winter begins, the birds and squirrels eat the art!
pages.brief: The Corn Palace is covered with grasses and corn in many colors. Birds and squirrels gather around the decorated building in winter, eating the colorful art as if the palace were the world’s largest bird feeder.

pages.text: Barney Smith’s Toilet Seat Art Museum Do you have an extra toilet seat? Bring it to Barney Smith’s Toilet Seat Art Museum. Barney Smith has made more than one thousand toilet seats into works of art.
pages.brief: Inside Barney Smith’s Toilet Seat Art Museum, more than a thousand toilet seats are displayed as works of art. Barney Smith stands among the decorated seats, showing the odd collection he has made from ordinary toilet seats.

pages.text: A big elephant needs a big drink of water. Lucy the Elephant The world’s largest elephant is a six- story building you can climb inside!
pages.brief: Lucy the Elephant, a six-story building shaped like a giant elephant, stands beside the road. Visitors can climb inside the enormous elephant, which is the world’s largest elephant and a surprising roadside sight to explore.

pages.text: Boll Weevil Monument A hundred years ago, a bug called the boll weevil destroyed cotton plants in Alabama. Farmers had to grow different plants. In the end, that helped the farmers. So they built a monument to the weevil.
pages.brief: A monument to the boll weevil stands in an Alabama town. Around it, cotton plants show what the bug destroyed, while different crops show what farmers grew instead. The farmers built the monument because the bug eventually helped them.

pages.text: Sign Post Forest The Sign Post Forest isn’t made of trees. It’s made of more than 100,000 signs. Do You Know? Not all roadside attractions are made by people. General Sherman Tree in Sequoia National Park is the world’s largest tree. It is thought to be between 2,300 and 2,700 years old.
pages.brief: A forest of signposts covered with thousands of signs stands beside a road. Nearby, a separate view shows the massive General Sherman Tree in Sequoia National Park, an ancient giant tree thought to be 2,300 to 2,700 years old.

pages.text: Inset: Stonehenge is a ring of stones raised 4,000 to 5,000 years ago. It is 90 miles west of London. Carhenge In Nebraska, you can visit a model of England’s Stonehenge. It wasn’t built with old stones, but with thirty-eight old cars.
pages.brief: Stonehenge is a ring of ancient standing stones raised 4,000 to 5,000 years ago, 90 miles west of London. In Nebraska, Carhenge copies its shape with thirty-eight old cars instead of stones. The two rings show the same form in very different materials.

pages.text: London Bridge London Bridge started out in London, England. Then an American bought the bridge. He spent a lot of money to have the bridge moved to Arizona.
pages.brief: London Bridge, a stone bridge with old arches, now stands in Arizona after an American bought it and spent a lot of money to move it from London, England. The bridge is shown in its new home.

pages.text: World’s Largest Basket Workers at a basket company get to work inside a basket that’s seven stories tall. When it was first built, a pilot flew his small plane through the handles!
pages.brief: A seven-story building shaped like a giant basket stands at a basket company. Workers are inside the basket building, and a small plane is shown flying through the basket’s enormous handles. The giant basket is the world’s largest basket.
