pages.text: There are five hands. Each hand has five fingers. You can add to find the total number of fingers. There are twenty-five fingers in all. Each group has the same number. So, you can also skip-count to find the total. There are twenty-five fingers in all. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Five hands are shown in the picture. Each hand has five fingers. The fingers are grouped by hand, and all five separate groups can be added or skip-counted to find the total number of fingers.

pages.text: There are five bugs in this picture. Each bug has six legs. You can add to find the total number of legs. There are thirty legs in all. Each bug has the same number of legs. So, you can also skip-count to find the total. You can solve this problem another way. You can multiply. There are thirty legs in all. You read it like this: five times six equals thirty. The number sentence means that you have five groups of six items, and the total is thirty. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Five bugs are shown in the picture. Each bug has six legs. The legs are grouped by bug, and the groups can be added, skip-counted, or multiplied as five times six to find thirty legs in all.

pages.text: There are thirty legs in all.
pages.brief: A picture shows thirty legs in all. The legs are arranged together so the total can be seen clearly as a single group. The image focuses only on the legs and their total number of legs.

pages.text: There are ten cars in this train. There are ten bears in each car. You can add to find the total number of bears. There are one hundred bears in all. You can also skip-count to find the total. You can solve this problem another way. You can multiply. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: A toy train is shown with ten cars. Each car holds ten bears. The bears are grouped by train car, and the groups can be added, skip-counted, or multiplied to find one hundred bears in all.

pages.text: You read it like this: ten times ten equals one hundred. The number sentence means that you have ten groups of ten items, and the total is one hundred. There are one hundred bears in all. 100 one hundred.
pages.brief: One hundred small toy bears are shown in all. The bears appear in ten equal groups of ten across the picture. Together, these groups present the full total of one hundred bears in the image.

pages.text: There are four pizzas. Each pizza is cut into six pieces. You can add to find the total number of pieces. There are twenty-four pieces in all. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Four pizzas are shown in the picture. Each pizza is cut into six pieces. The pieces are grouped by pizza, and the groups can be added to find the total number of all pizza pieces.

pages.text: You can also skip-count to find the total. There are twenty-four pieces of pizza in all.
pages.brief: The pizza pieces are shown again in the picture. There are four pizzas, each cut into six pieces. Because the groups are equal, the pieces can be skip-counted to find twenty-four pieces of pizza in all.

pages.text: Which container has more objects? You can skip-count to find the total. Think of the container as an array. An array shows objects in rows and columns. There are two rows. There are six eggs in each row. You can write a multiplication sentence to find the total number of eggs. There are four rows. There are three limes in each row. You can write a multiplication sentence to find the total number of limes. 4 x 3 = 12 Both containers hold twelve objects. Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Two containers are shown side by side. One container holds eggs in two rows of six. The other holds limes in four rows of three. Both containers can be seen as arrays, and each holds twelve objects.

pages.text: There are six ways you can arrange twelve in arrays. Here are all the other ways you can arrange twelve in arrays.
pages.brief: Several arrays of twelve objects are shown in the picture. Each array uses a different number of rows and columns. Together they show the six ways twelve objects can be arranged in rows and columns.

pages.text: What number sentences could you write about these arrays? Real Life Multiplication.
pages.brief: Several different arrays of objects are shown in the picture for students to examine. The objects are arranged in rows and columns. The arrays are displayed so number sentences could be written about each one.

books.title: Karate
books.art_why: Karate classes, dojos, students and belts exist in the real world today, so photographs show them clearly.

pages.text: What Is Karate? Karate is a martial art in which people don’t use weapons. The word karate means “empty hand” in Japanese.
pages.brief: A group of karate students in a bright dojo practice empty-handed strikes and blocks, wearing training robes and standing barefoot on the mat. No weapons are anywhere in the room; their open hands and focused faces show karate as a martial art done with the body alone.

pages.text: Many people believe that karate began in the 1600s on Okinawa (oh-kee-NAH-wah), an island between China and Japan. The people who lived on the island could not have weapons. They came up with karate as a way to defend themselves. Now, karate is popular all around the world.
pages.brief: On the island of Okinawa, between China and Japan, islanders in simple old-style clothing practice self-defense moves with bare hands in an open village space. Green hills and sea lie behind them, suggesting the island setting where people defended themselves long ago.

pages.text: The Gym Karate students train at a dojo, or gym. When they enter a dojo, they bow their heads to show good manners. The karate teacher is called a sensei. The sensei has many lessons to pass on. Students learn to listen to their sensei and follow the rules of the dojo.
pages.brief: Students file into a dojo and bow their heads toward their sensei, a karate teacher standing calmly at the front. The teacher gestures as students kneel and listen, following the rules of the training hall, with mats and a clean wooden floor around them.

pages.text: Belts Students have to wear the right clothes before they start to train. In the dojo, they wear a special robe, or gi, with a colored belt around the waist. Students move on to different colored belts as they train and gain new skills. However, getting a new belt isn’t just about learning new moves.
pages.brief: Karate students stand in a row wearing white training robes, each with a colored belt tied around the waist. One student adjusts a belt while others watch; different colored belts show the skills each student has earned through training.

pages.text: While students earn belts, they learn many good habits, such as self-control and patience. They can use these skills in other areas of their lives. The good habits students learn are just as important as the moves they practice.
pages.brief: Students sit quietly on the dojo floor with straight backs and calm faces, practicing patience and self-control. One child waits while a partner holds a pose; others show steady focus, demonstrating good habits learned in karate that carry into everyday life.

pages.text: Students earn new colored belts in a certain order. One story tells the meaning of each color through the growth of a plant. The different colors of the belts stand for the colors of the plant, the Sun, and the sky. A student grows much like a young plant. They grow as time passes and gain more skills.
pages.brief: A young green plant grows beside a row of colored karate belts laid out in order, with the sun and blue sky above. Students stand nearby in their gi, comparing the plant's growth and the belt colors that stand for the plant, sun, and sky.

pages.text: Learning Karate Students learn karate in three main steps: kihon, kata, and kumite.
pages.brief: Karate students practice three kinds of training in the dojo: one beginner holds a low stance, another moves through a set routine, and two others face each other with controlled techniques. The sensei watches, showing the three main steps of learning karate.

pages.text: Kihon Kihon is the set of moves for beginners. In learn to breathe stand in the right position. They also learn how to do kicks, punches, blocks, and other moves. It is important for them to learn patience. Students practice until they are perfect.
pages.brief: Beginners in white gi practice kihon, standing in the correct position with feet planted and hands ready. One student breathes slowly while others practice kicks, punches, and blocks in the air, repeating each move again and again with patient, careful effort.

pages.text: Kata Kata is putting the moves from kihon into a routine. Students pretend to fight off attackers and learn to defend themselves. They also practice their flow from one move to the next. There are many different katas to learn.
pages.brief: A student moves through a kata routine on the dojo mat, stepping and turning as if fighting off imaginary attackers, hands striking and blocking in a smooth flow. Other students watch and copy the same sequence of moves, practicing defense and the flow from one move to the next.

pages.text: Many students also practice bunkai while learning kata. In bunkai, students learn why the moves from kata are useful. They learn to slow down and think about each move before they do it.
pages.brief: A student pauses in the middle of a kata, slowing down to think about each move before doing it. The sensei stands nearby explaining with open hands, while the student studies the position of a blocking arm, learning why the movement is useful.

pages.text: Kumite After a lot of hard work, karate students reach the last step. In kumite, they use everything they have learned by practicing moves on one another.
pages.brief: Two karate students face each other on the mat and practice kumite, using the moves they have learned on one another with controlled punches and blocks. Their sensei watches closely as they step and respond, showing their hard work at the final stage of training.

pages.text: Conclusion For many years, people around the world have learned good habits through karate. They have also worked hard to become stronger and faster, and to earn new belts. Some students hope to become karate masters, and everyone has a lot of fun trying to get there.
pages.brief: Karate students of different ages train together in the dojo, some practicing moves, some tying belts, and all smiling as they work hard to become stronger, faster, and more skilled. A few look toward their sensei, hoping to become karate masters one day.

books.title: The Butterfly Life Cycle
books.art_why: Monarch butterflies and their real-life life-cycle stages can be photographed.

pages.text: The Life Cycle A monarch butterfly has four stages in its life cycle. They are egg, caterpillar, pupa, and adult.
pages.brief: A monarch butterfly rests near the four stages of its life cycle: an oval egg on a leaf, a caterpillar eating, a green pupa hanging from a branch, and an adult monarch butterfly with open wings.

pages.text: Egg A female monarch butterfly lays an egg on the bottom of a leaf. She might lay several hundred eggs in her lifetime. The eggs are oval shaped. A caterpillar grows inside the tiny egg. The egg hatches in three to twelve days.
pages.brief: A female monarch butterfly clings to the underside of a leaf and lays an oval egg. The tiny egg holds a growing caterpillar inside. Nearby, more eggs show she may lay several hundred in her lifetime.

pages.text: The hungry caterpillar eats all the time. It needs a lot of food to grow. First, the caterpillar eats its own eggshell. Then, the caterpillar eats the leaf it is on.
pages.brief: A hungry caterpillar sits on a leaf and eats all the time. It first chews its own empty eggshell nearby, then turns to the leaf beneath it, taking big bites to get food for growth.

pages.text: The caterpillar grows quickly, but its skin does not grow. The caterpillar’s old skin splits and peels away. The caterpillar will shed the old skin many times in this stage.
pages.brief: A growing caterpillar clings to a leaf as its old skin splits and peels away. The tight old skin separates from its body, showing that the caterpillar will shed this covering many times during this stage.

pages.text: Do You Know? New skin is under the old skin. It is soft at first but soon hardens. The caterpillar sheds its skin four to six times and eats the old skin each time. The caterpillar grows for two to four weeks.
pages.brief: A close view shows a caterpillar with soft new skin under peeling old skin. The new skin is soft at first. Beside it, the caterpillar eats a shed skin, one of four to six times it sheds and eats.

pages.text: Pupa When the caterpillar is grown, it hangs from a branch to prepare for the next stage. It sheds its skin one last time. The new skin is bright green and looks like a leaf.
pages.brief: A grown caterpillar hangs from a branch, ready for the next stage. It sheds its skin one last time. The new skin is bright green and shaped like a leaf, covering the caterpillar as it prepares to change.

pages.text: This green skin hardens around the caterpillar. It will protect it from other animals as it changes inside. The caterpillar becomes a pupa. It will stay inside its shell for one to two weeks. During this time, big changes happen to its body.
pages.brief: A bright green shell hardens around the caterpillar, now a pupa, hanging from a branch. The leaf-like shell protects it from other animals while big changes happen inside its body over one to two weeks.

pages.text: Adult Butterfly An adult butterfly comes out of the shell. Its wet wings are folded against its body.
pages.brief: A newly emerged adult monarch butterfly comes out of its pupa shell on a branch. Its wet wings stay folded tightly against its body as it rests quietly, still clinging to the empty shell nearby.

pages.text: The new butterfly rests. The butterfly must hang upside down, or it will not be able to fly. Blood pumping into the wings causes them to unfold and spread out.
pages.brief: A new butterfly hangs upside down from a branch and rests. Blood pumps into its wings, causing them to unfold and spread out. It must keep hanging this way, or it will not be able to fly.

pages.text: The butterfly hangs for several hours. The sun and air dry its delicate wings. A butterfly has two pairs of wings. They are covered in scales. The wings in the front often have a different pattern from the pair in the back. The colors on the wings are usually similar to each other.
pages.brief: A monarch butterfly hangs in the sunshine for several hours while the sun and air dry its delicate wings. Its two pairs of wings are covered in scales, with different patterns on the front and back pairs but similar colors.

pages.text: Once the butterfly is able to fly, it flies off to eat. Unlike a caterpillar, a butterfly does not eat leaves. Instead, it sips sweet liquid from flowers. It also searches for a mate.
pages.brief: A monarch butterfly flies off from its resting place to eat. It hovers at a flower and sips sweet liquid instead of eating leaves. Nearby, it searches for a mate among the flowers and leaves.

pages.text: Adult butterflies do not grow. They save their energy for flying and laying eggs. Females are bigger than males. A monarch butterfly may only live for two to six weeks. After she finds a mate, the female monarch lays her eggs. The butterfly life cycle starts all over again.
pages.brief: A larger female monarch butterfly lays eggs on a leaf while a smaller male rests nearby. The adults save their energy for flying and laying eggs. Their life cycle starts all over again with the new eggs.

books.title: Stonehenge
books.art_why: Stonehenge was built thousands of years ago, so no photographs of its construction exist.

pages.text: An Ancient Monument There is an ancient monument in England that is made of dirt and giant stones. It is called Stonehenge, and it was built thousands of years ago. Scientists called archaeologists have been studying it for a long time. They are trying to learn how and why it was built. They also want to know more about the people who built it.
pages.brief: A wide view of Stonehenge in England, a huge ancient monument of dirt and giant standing stones in an open field. Two archaeologists study the stones, watching closely and trying to understand how and why ancient people built the monument and who they were.

pages.text: Earth and Giant Stones From the sky, Stonehenge looks like a small circle inside a big circle. The bigger circle is a ditch around a raised mound of dirt. The giant stones in the outer circle are made of a type of sandstone. Stones called lintels once lay atop the giant stones to connect them all together. The inner stones are made of three parts, and they form a horseshoe shape. Two stones stand upright, and one lintel lies across them. Other rocks in the circle are made of bluestone.
pages.brief: Seen from above, Stonehenge shows a small circle inside a bigger circle. The outer ring is a ditch around a raised dirt mound. Giant sandstone stones stand in the outer circle, with lintels resting across them. Inner stones form a horseshoe shape, two uprights with one lintel, and other bluestones nearby.

pages.text: Where Is Stonehenge? Stonehenge sits in an open field in southern England. Experts say people have been living in that area for about ten thousand years. The settlement may have been one of the biggest in England at one time. Long ago, the area was covered in trees. People cut them down to clear land for farming.
pages.brief: Stonehenge stands in an open field in southern England. In the distance, an ancient settlement shows where many people once lived. At the edge of the field, people cut down trees to clear land for farming, while the monument waits among the cleared ground.

pages.text: Building Stonehenge Experts believe that people started building Stonehenge about five thousand years ago. Back then, people only had simple stone tools, not powerful machines. They did almost everything with their minds and muscles. The stones must have been brought to Stonehenge from far away. Tests have been done to prove it was possible to move the stones to Stonehenge. Stones were put on wooden sleds and dragged on greased with animal fat.
pages.brief: Ancient builders with simple stone tools drag a huge stone on a wooden sled across greased ground. Ropes pull the sled while people use their muscles to move it. The heavy stone is being brought from far away to Stonehenge, showing how people moved stones without powerful machines.

pages.text: Lifting the must have been very hard. Experts think the have dug holes and then tipped the bottoms of the stones into the holes. Then they could be pulled upright using ropes. Workers might have slid the tops of the arches up ramps built of dirt and wood. Then the tops could be set on the standing stones. No one knows for sure how the builders built Stonehenge. They did not leave pictures or writing to explain how they did it. That is why Stonehenge is still a big mystery.
pages.brief: Workers dig holes and tip the bottoms of giant stones into them. Others pull ropes to haul the stones upright. A long ramp of dirt and wood rises beside the standing stones, and workers slide a lintel up the ramp to set it across the tops of the arches.

pages.text: An Outdoor Temple Why was Stonehenge built? Archaeologists continue to look and dig for clues about its purpose. One clue is that it was built away from where most people lived. Experts think Stonehenge was a temple of some kind. People probably came there for special events. They might have visited to remember dead relatives.
pages.brief: Archaeologists dig and search for clues beside Stonehenge, an open-air temple set away from where most people lived. In the distance, small groups of ancient people gather at the monument for a special event, perhaps to remember dead relatives. The wide field surrounds the great stones.

pages.text: Stonehenge was also a graveyard. Archaeologists have found the bodies of about 240 people nearby.
pages.brief: Near Stonehenge, archaeologists carefully uncover buried remains in the ground. The bones of about 240 people lie in the earth around the monument. The great stones stand above, showing that Stonehenge was also a graveyard where ancient people were buried long ago.

pages.text: Another idea about Stonehenge is that it lines up with the sun’s movements. The sun shines through certain parts of the monument when the seasons change. This was important information for farmers long ago. It helped them figure out the best time to plant their crops.
pages.brief: The sun shines through certain parts of Stonehenge as the seasons change. Ancient farmers watch the light and use it to judge the best time to plant their crops. Around the monument, fields stretch out, and the standing stones line up with the sun’s movement across the sky.

pages.text: Stonehenge Today More than nine hundred thousand people visit Stonehenge each year. The visitor center has stone tools and other ancient objects. There are huts to show what life was like long ago. Volunteers show visitors ancient skills such as pottery and rope making.
pages.brief: Modern visitors walk around Stonehenge and explore the visitor center. Inside, stone tools and ancient objects are on display. Outside, round huts show what life was like long ago. A volunteer sits nearby making pottery and twisting rope, showing visitors ancient skills used by people long ago.

pages.text: Archaeologists continue to explore the Stonehenge site. They use new tools such as radar that can find objects underground. This helps them make more discoveries faster.
pages.brief: Archaeologists explore the Stonehenge site with a new radar tool. They move the device over the ground, searching for objects buried underground. Beneath the soil, shapes of hidden things appear, helping the archaeologists make discoveries faster while the ancient stones stand in the background.

pages.text: Ancient Wonder No one knows for sure why ancient people built Stonehenge. How they did it is also a mystery. Still, Stonehenge continues to fill people with wonder thousands of years after it was built.
pages.brief: Stonehenge stands under a wide sky, thousands of years after it was built. Visitors look at the ancient stones with wonder. No one knows for sure why it was built or how the builders did it, yet the mystery still draws people to the monument.

books.title: Canada
books.art_why: Canada today has real cities, people, animals and landscapes that can be photographed.

pages.text: Where Is It? Canada is the biggest country in North America. It is so big that it reaches from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean. Canada is farther north than most other countries.
pages.brief: A wide satellite-style view of Canada stretching across northern North America, from the Atlantic Ocean on one side to the Pacific Ocean on the other. The land sits far north, with cold northern areas visible above the main landmass.

pages.text: Canada has only one neighbor, the United States. Ottawa is the country’s capital. The city’s buildings are fun to visit.
pages.brief: Several visitors walking among Ottawa’s city buildings, exploring the capital’s streets. A border line separates Canada from its only neighbor, the United States, nearby. The view shows Canada’s capital city and the United States beside it.

pages.text: People Nearly all Canadians speak French, English, or both. Canada’s Indigenous peoples include more than 600 groups of First Nations. They also include the Inuit and Métis. People come from faraway countries to live in Canada.
pages.brief: A diverse group of Canadians talking together, including First Nations, Inuit, and Métis people. Some speak French, some English, some both. Newcomers from faraway countries stand with them, showing the many peoples who live in Canada.

pages.text: Together, all of these different people make Canada strong. Most Canadians live in big cities in the south of Canada. Few people live in the far north.
pages.brief: Many Canadians gathered in a busy southern city with streets and buildings, while only a few people appear in a far northern settlement. The crowded city and the quiet north show that most Canadians live in big cities in the south.

pages.text: Land Canada has many different landforms. In the west are rows of steep mountains. Then there are flat or rolling plains. A high, flat area with thousands of lakes is in the middle.
pages.brief: Steep mountain ranges rise in rows across western Canada. Flat and rolling plains spread out beside them. In the middle, a high, flat area holds thousands of small lakes, showing several of Canada’s different landforms.

pages.text: The land in the south is where most of the cities are. In the east are hills. In the north, the land is covered with ice and snow.
pages.brief: Big cities fill the southern land, with streets and buildings. Hills rise in the east. In the north, ice and snow cover the ground. The wide scene shows Canada’s south, east, and far north side by side.

pages.text: Animals Some animals live only in the cold north. Others live only in the mountains or forests. Polar bears and harp seals live in the north. They both have white fur to hide on the snow.
pages.brief: A polar bear and a harp seal rest on snow in Canada’s cold north. Both have white fur that blends into the snowy ground, helping them hide. Nearby, a forest and mountain edge show where other animals live.

pages.text: Big sheep and goats live in the mountains. They have feet that help them climb rocks. Many animals in Canada move in winter and spring. Canada geese fly south every winter. They return in the spring when it is warmer.
pages.brief: Big sheep and goats stand on rocky mountain slopes, their feet gripping the rocks as they climb. Above them, Canada geese fly south in winter. In spring, the geese return north when the weather grows warmer.

pages.text: Celebrations All across Canada, people celebrate winter. There are festivals for ice-skating and ice carving. There are dogsled races across the snow.
pages.brief: A crowd of people celebrate winter across Canada. Some skate on ice, others carve ice sculptures, and a dogsled race crosses the snow. The outdoor festival scene shows different winter games and activities in the cold.

pages.text: The biggest winter festival is in Quebec City. There is an ice castle to visit and games to play.
pages.brief: Quebec City hosts the biggest winter festival. Visitors explore an ice castle and play games in the cold, snowy city. The scene shows the festival’s ice castle and groups of people enjoying winter games outdoors.

pages.text: Conclusion Canada is a very big country with many different landforms and animals. It has many different people, too. Canadians say their differences make them strong.
pages.brief: A wide view of Canada brings together steep mountains, plains, lakes, ice and snow, animals, and many different people standing together in one scene. The diverse group shows how Canadians say their differences make them strong.

pages.text: Population: 38,000,000 Land: 9,984,670 square kilometers (3,855,103 sq. mi.) Capital City: Ottawa Official Languages: English and French Currency: Canadian dollar.
pages.brief: Ottawa’s city buildings rise in the capital, with Canadian dollar coins and banknotes in the foreground. Nearby, people talk in English and French. A broad view of Canada’s land stretches out, suggesting the country’s huge land area.

books.title: Rainbows
books.art_why: Keyword check suggests drawing for this rainbow science book.

pages.text: Introduction When the Sun comes out after it rains, run outside. You may see a rainbow in the sky.
pages.brief: A child runs outside onto open ground just after rain, looking up at a bright sky. The Sun shines through clearing clouds, and a colorful rainbow arcs above. The ground looks wet from the recent rain.

pages.text: Rainbows are tricks made by light. We can see them, but we can’t touch them or walk around them. They seem to move away when we try to get close to them. Science can explain how rainbows happen.
pages.brief: A rainbow hangs in the sky above open land, bright and untouchable. A child stands below and reaches toward it but cannot touch it or walk around it. As the child moves closer, the rainbow seems to shift farther away.

pages.text: Where and When Rainbows Appear Look around the next time you see a rainbow. The Sun will be shining from behind you. There will be rain in front of you, where you’ll see the rainbow.
pages.brief: A person stands outdoors with the Sun shining behind them and rain falling in front. Ahead, a rainbow appears in the rainy sky. The scene shows the Sun behind the viewer and rain ahead, where the rainbow is seen.

pages.text: Rainbows need water drops and sunlight to form. They can even form under a bright moon. These are called moonbows.
pages.brief: Sunlight passes into water drops in the air, forming a rainbow. In a separate night scene, a bright moon shines above, and water drops and moonlight form a moonbow. Both scenes show water drops and light working together in the sky.

pages.text: We usually see a rainbow as a half circle. It actually forms a full circle. From the ground, we can only see the top half.
pages.brief: A rainbow appears as a half circle above the ground. Higher in the sky, the same rainbow is shown as a complete circle. From the ground, a viewer can see only the top half of the full circle.

pages.text: How Rainbows Form Years ago, a French scientist studied rainbows. He found that to see a rainbow, you must be in the right spot. Rainbows in Myths and Tales.
pages.brief: Years ago, a French scientist studies a rainbow in an old-fashioned setting, observing where it appears in the sky. He stands in the right spot to see it, studying how rainbows happen and what makes them visible.

pages.text: Knowing how rainbows. Think of running on land. Now think of trying to run through water. You will move because it is thicker than air. In the same way, light moves faster through air than through water. As the light moves through water, it slows down and bends.
pages.brief: A person runs on land, then tries to run through water and slows down. Nearby, a beam of light travels through air and then enters water, where it slows and bends. The scene compares movement through air and water with light bending in water.

pages.text: The Colors of the Rainbow 1 Sunlight is made up of many colors. Water drops split the sunlight into different colors. Splitting light makes a rainbow. 2 You have to be in the right spot to see a rainbow. Each water drop 1 reflects colored light at a slightly 2 different angle. 3 Rainbows form when water drops meet sunlight. The light bends.
pages.brief: Sunlight enters water drops and splits into many colors. Each drop reflects colored light at a slightly different angle. A viewer stands in the right spot as water drops meet sunlight, and the bent light forms a rainbow of separate colors in the sky.

pages.text: The colors of the rainbow always appear in the same order. The name ROY G. BIV can help you remember the seven main colors. They are red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. Make Your Own Rainbow.
pages.brief: A rainbow arc shows seven colors in their usual order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. The bands appear in the same sequence along the curve, making the colors easy to see from one side to the other.

pages.text: Conclusion Rain stops and the Sun comes out. A beautiful rainbow sweeps across the sky. Most people find it hard not to stop and stare when a rainbow appears.
pages.brief: Rain stops, the Sun comes out, and a beautiful rainbow sweeps across the sky. Several people outdoors stop and stare up at the colorful arc, finding it hard not to pause and look at the sight.

pages.text: Science explains how rainbows form. Still, a rainbow is always a magical sight to see.
pages.brief: A rainbow arcs across the sky above open land. People below look up at it, taking in the magical sight. Even with science explaining how rainbows form, the rainbow remains beautiful and wondrous to see.

books.title: Petra
books.art_why: The book covers the ancient Nabataeans and construction over 2,000 years ago, so scenes need drawings.

pages.text: Rock City More than two thousand years ago, a group of people built an amazing city in the Middle East. They used special tools to carve buildings out of mountains. These people were the Nabataeans (nab-uh-TEE-uns). Their beautiful rock city was Petra.
pages.brief: Nabataean workers use special tools to carve tall buildings directly out of a mountain in the Middle East, shaping a beautiful rock city. The buildings rise from the rock face as the workers cut and smooth the stone around them.

pages.text: Petra SYRIA IRAQ Amman DEAD SEA ISRAEL JORDAN Petra EUROPE ASIA EGYPT Ma’an AFRICA RED SEA SAUDI ARABIA City in the Desert Petra is in the country of Jordan, in one of Earth’s driest deserts. Red sandstone cliffs and canyons are all that can be seen for many miles. A canyon called the Siq (SEEK) leads to Petra. It is the main way to reach the city. the Siq.
pages.brief: A dry desert in Jordan stretches out with red sandstone cliffs and canyons for many miles. A narrow canyon called the Siq cuts between high rock walls, forming the main route that leads toward the hidden city of Petra.

pages.text: Buried City The city of Petra is 264 square kilometers (102 sq. mi.). The downtown area is 6 square kilometers (2 sq. mi.). The city has hundreds of tombs and other structures. Most of Petra is still buried under the ground. Scientists find more structures as they dig it up. Colonnaded Street.
pages.brief: The buried city of Petra spreads across a wide area, with hundreds of tombs and other structures. Some structures stand exposed while much of Petra remains under the ground. Scientists dig in the earth, uncovering more structures as they work.

pages.text: The Treasury is the first structure visitors see after they pass through the Siq. The Treasury is Petra’s best-known structure. The Royal Tombs are where they buried their kings. Other famous structures include the Theatre, Petra Museum, and the Monastery. Many structures are over 30 meters (100 ft.) tall. The Nabataeans also made many structures to collect, store, and carry water. They could not have lived in such a dry place without a way to get and hold water.
pages.brief: The Treasury stands as the first structure visitors see after passing through the Siq. The Royal Tombs hold buried kings, and other famous structures include the Theatre, Petra Museum, and the Monastery. Tall structures rise over thirty meters. Nabataean water structures collect, store, and carry water.

pages.text: A Journey Through Petra Entrance to the Siq Visitor Centre Path through the Siq Treasury Street of Facades Theatre Royal Tombs Colonnaded Street Monastery Petra Museum Walking east to west from the Visitor Centre to the Monastery takes about twenty minutes at a normal pace. Most visitors take much longer, though, as they stop to look at each new place.
pages.brief: A route through Petra runs east to west from the Visitor Centre through the Siq, past the Treasury, Street of Facades, Theatre, Royal Tombs, Colonnaded Street, and Monastery, ending near Petra Museum. Visitors walk the path and stop to look at each new place.

pages.text: A Busy Trade Center Long ago, people from the Middle East, Asia, and Africa crossed the desert to trade with each other. They traveled through the land where the Nabataeans lived. The Nabataeans took care of camels, goats, and sheep. At first, they wandered from place to place. Later, they grew rich, settled down, and built Petra. Scientists think the Nabataeans built the Rose City around 300 bce. Over time, it became a busy trade center.
pages.brief: Long ago, people from the Middle East, Asia, and Africa cross the desert to trade. Nabataeans care for camels, goats, and sheep, wandering from place to place. Later they grow rich, settle down, and build Petra, which becomes a busy trade center.

pages.text: Not much is known about the Nabataeans, but it is known that they worshipped the Sun. Scientists know this from studying Petra’s most important structures. On certain days of the year, the Sun lights up special parts of these structures. The Nabataeans must have built them on purpose so the Sun would shine on them that way.
pages.brief: Nabataeans worship the Sun at Petra’s most important structures. On certain days of the year, sunlight shines into special parts of the structures. The builders made them on purpose so the Sun would light them that way.

pages.text: The Romans had a big empire based in Italy. Romans took over Petra in 106 ce. People’s lives mostly stayed the same. They built new structures that looked more like Roman structures. A huge earthquake in 363 ce broke Petra’s water system. People started leaving the city at that time. Another big earthquake happened in 551. Arabs took over Petra about a hundred years later. The last people left Petra soon after.
pages.brief: Romans take over Petra in 106 ce, and people’s lives mostly stay the same. New structures look more Roman. A huge earthquake in 363 ce breaks Petra’s water system, and people begin leaving. Another earthquake hits in 551, Arabs take over about a hundred years later, and the last people leave soon after.

pages.text: Building Petra Many of Petra’s structures are carved right into the mountains. Others are built from sandstone taken from the mountains. A few structures use both methods. Scientists are certain that Petra’s carved structures were made from the top down. They know this because some structures were never finished. They are only carved at the top. No one knows for sure how the Nabataeans made the carved structures. Some scientists think they removed large blocks of sandstone, leaving huge rock steps. Carvers would have stood on the steps as they worked up high.
pages.brief: Many of Petra’s structures are carved into mountains, while others are built from sandstone taken from the mountains. Some use both methods. Carved structures were made from the top down; unfinished ones are carved only at the top. Scientists think workers removed large blocks, leaving rock steps for carvers to stand on.

pages.text: Other scientists think the carvers put strong pins into the rock. Then they rested a wooden board on the pins. They would have stood on the board while they worked. Scientists hope to learn more as they keep studying Petra.
pages.brief: Other scientists think carvers put strong pins into the rock and rested a wooden board on the pins. The carvers stood on the board while they worked high on the rock face. Scientists keep studying Petra to learn more about how the structures were made.

pages.text: Seeing Petra More than four hundred thousand people visit Petra each year. No cars are allowed, so many people walk through the Siq to get there. Others ride a horse, donkey, or camel. Visitors walk around Petra on their own. It can take up to five days to see everything!
pages.brief: More than four hundred thousand people visit Petra each year. No cars are allowed, so many walk through the Siq, while others ride a horse, donkey, or camel. Visitors walk around Petra on their own, and seeing everything can take up to five days.

pages.text: New Discoveries Scientists learn more about Petra all the time. Not long ago, they found pools, gardens, and fountains. Every discovery shows more about how smart the Nabataeans were. They figured out how to bring water to a very dry desert. Long ago, people came to Petra because of water. More than two thousand years later, they come to see a beautiful rock city.
pages.brief: Scientists keep learning about Petra. They recently found pools, gardens, and fountains. Each discovery shows how smart the Nabataeans were, figuring out how to bring water to a very dry desert. Long ago people came to Petra for water; now they come to see a beautiful rock city.

books.title: Slithery Snakes
books.art_why: Real snakes and their features exist, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Introduction Snakes are reptiles. There are several thousand kinds of snakes. They live in oceans, in trees, and on land, and they survive in unusual ways.
pages.brief: Several kinds of snakes are shown in the ocean, in trees, and on land, each surviving in its own unusual way; a group of reptiles with long bodies appears in each habitat. A close view shows one snake among tree branches and another moving across open ground.

pages.text: Wild snakes live almost everywhere on Earth except Antarctica and some islands. Some wild snakes may live as long as twenty-five years. Biggest and Smallest.
pages.brief: Wild snakes are shown in many natural places on Earth, on land and near islands, but none in a snowy Antarctic landscape; a very large snake and a very small snake are placed near each other.

pages.text: Snake Traits Snakes are cold-blooded. Their body temperature changes with the temperature around them. Snakes find sunshine to stay warm. They find shade to stay cool. During winter, some snakes stay underground or under rock piles to stay warm. Snakes also rest in groups to share body heat.
pages.brief: Snakes are shown warming themselves in sunshine and cooling in shade; some rest underground or under rock piles during winter, while a group of snakes rests together to share body heat, their bodies close to the ground.

pages.text: Snakes have long backbones. Their backbones have many separate bones, which lets them move in many ways. A snake’s body is covered in scales. The scales protect it. They also help keep the snake dry. The scales grow from its skin. Snakes use their scales and muscles to move. The scales on their belly grab the surface beneath them. Their muscles help them move along the ground. Some snakes even use their muscles and scales to climb trees.
pages.brief: A close view shows a snake’s long backbone made of many separate bones, and its body covered in scales; another snake uses belly scales to grip the ground while its muscles bend and push it forward, and one climbs a tree.

pages.text: Snake scales look like a single sheet of skin. Snakes don’t shed skin. Instead, they shed the outer layers of their scales up to four times per year. This is called molting. When molting, snakes rub against something like a rock or log. This helps their outer layer stretch and split. Young snakes shed more because they grow fast. Snakes also shed to get rid of pests on their scales.
pages.brief: A snake rubs against a rough rock and a log, its outer scale layers stretching and splitting as it molts; a smaller young snake nearby also sheds scales, and loose old skin is left behind.

pages.text: Snakes have clear scales instead of eyelids. The scales keep their eyes from drying out. Snakes cannot blink. Snakes do not have ears you can see. Instead, sound passes through their jaws to their inner ears, which sends the sound to their brain.
pages.brief: A close view of a snake’s eye shows a clear scale instead of an eyelid, keeping the eye from drying out; the snake cannot blink, and another view shows its jaw area where sound passes inward toward its inner ears.

pages.text: Another important feature of a snake is its tongue. Snakes use their tongue to smell. Smells in the air stick to their tongue. They identify the smell using special sacs behind their nose. Some snakes can sense the heat of animals nearby. Pits near the snake’s eyes sense heat. These snakes can tell how far away something is in the dark when they hunt.
pages.brief: A snake flicks its tongue into the air to catch smells, then uses special sacs behind its nose to identify them; a close view shows heat pits near its eyes as it hunts in the dark and judges distance.

pages.text: Hunting and Eating Snakes are meat eaters. Some snakes inject venom when biting prey. Other snakes squeeze prey to death. Some snakes swallow prey alive. Most snakes’ jaws are loosely connected. This lets snakes open their mouth wide to swallow large prey. Snakes’ fangs and other teeth point backward, helping push food toward their throat. Snakes have a breathing tube that they push out of their mouth. This lets them breathe when they swallow prey. Muscles move it to the stomach. Stomach acids turn prey into liquid so the snake can digest it easier.
pages.brief: A snake opens its loosely connected jaws wide to swallow large prey, while backward-pointing teeth push food toward its throat; another injects venom when biting prey, one squeezes prey, and another pushes a breathing tube out of its mouth.

pages.text: How Snakes Are Born Most female snakes that live in cold areas lay eggs in late spring or early summer. Snakes that live in warmer areas may mate at any time of year. Baby snakes may grow sharp teeth to cut through the eggs. Once they hatch, they must survive on their own and face many dangers. Some female snakes keep eggs inside their body until they hatch. Then they give birth to live babies.
pages.brief: A female snake in a cold area lays eggs in late spring or early summer; babies use sharp teeth to cut through the eggs and then face dangers on their own, while another female keeps eggs inside until live babies are born.

pages.text: Venomous Snakes Venom is a dangerous liquid. Some snakes inject venom when they bite with their fangs. Venom is made in sacs behind the snake’s eyes. It flows through the snake’s fangs from these sacs.
pages.brief: A close view of a venomous snake’s head shows its fangs and the sacs behind its eyes where venom is made; the dangerous liquid flows from those sacs through the fangs when the snake bites.

pages.text: Snakes use venom to defend and attack. Snakes usually inject more venom when biting in defense. The venom paralyzes their prey. Some snakes inject venom and let the prey go. Then they follow the prey until it dies. Other snakes use their teeth or body to hold on to prey until it dies. Then they eat it. Venom versus Poison.
pages.brief: A snake bites in defense and injects venom, then follows prey it has let go until the prey dies; another snake uses its teeth or body to hold on to prey until it dies, then eats it.

pages.text: Conclusion Snakes are amazing hunters. They have survived almost everywhere. Snakes are unusual animals that play an important role in our environment.
pages.brief: Several snakes are shown as hunters in different natural surroundings, moving through land, trees, and water; one snake catches prey while others move quietly through their habitats, showing how they survive almost everywhere and play a role in the environment.

books.title: Istanbul
books.art_why: The book focuses on empires, rulers and very old structures from long ago.

pages.text: One City, Two Worlds A ship sails into the port of a big city. It came from Europe and is on its way to Asia. This is Istanbul, Turkey. Parts of this Wowser! amazing city are on each continent.
pages.brief: A ship sails into the port of a big city, having come from Europe and on its way to Asia. This is Istanbul, Turkey, where parts of the city lie on each continent across the water.

pages.text: Where in the World? Istanbul is in the northwest corner of Turkey. It is on both sides of a narrow waterway between two seas. Istanbul has the most people of any city in Europe.
pages.brief: A view of Istanbul shows the city in the northwest corner of Turkey, set on both sides of a narrow waterway between two seas. Dense city areas line the waterway, showing why Istanbul has the most people of any city in Europe.

pages.text: History Istanbul has been an important port since long ago. It is on the only road between the two seas. People from both the East and West come to Istanbul for many reasons.
pages.brief: Long ago and today, ships from the East and West arrive at Istanbul’s port, which sits on the only road between two seas. People from both directions come to the city for many different reasons.

pages.text: Istanbul has had many rulers and has been a capital of many empires. Its name has changed several times. It became Istanbul in 1930. Many buildings and parts of the city have been destroyed and built again. Let’s visit some interesting places in Istanbul. Istanbul’s Other Names.
pages.brief: Istanbul’s long history includes many rulers and empires, and the city was once a capital. Its name changed several times before it became Istanbul in 1930. Buildings and parts of the city were destroyed and built again.

pages.text: Water Tank This huge underground water tank is no longer used. Long ago, it was the most important water supply for the city. The water came from a lake. Istanbul has many very old water tanks. This one is the biggest.
pages.brief: A huge underground water tank stretches out below the city, no longer used today. Long ago it was the most important water supply for Istanbul, filled with water from a lake. It is the biggest of the city’s many very old water tanks.

pages.text: Covered Market This huge covered market is made of stone. The first parts were built in 1461, and other parts were added over time. Today, it has sixty-one covered streets and more than four thousand shops. Shops sell clothing, jewelry, rugs, and many other things. Wowser!
pages.brief: A huge covered market built of stone spreads through many streets, with new parts added over time since 1461. Today it has sixty-one covered streets and more than four thousand shops selling clothing, jewelry, rugs, and many other things.

pages.text: Island Tower This tower is on a small island in Istanbul’s waterway. It was built about 2,400 years ago. Long ago, people used the tower to watch ships passing by. Later, the tower was a lighthouse. Today, it is a restaurant. Do You Know?
pages.brief: A tower stands on a small island in Istanbul’s waterway. It was built about 2,400 years ago, and long ago people used it to watch ships passing by. Later it was a lighthouse; today it is a restaurant.

pages.text: Tall Tower This tall tower was built in 1348. The tower was first used as a lighthouse. Later, it was a prison. Then, people used it to watch for fires. Today, people visit the tower to look out over Istanbul.
pages.brief: A tall tower rises above Istanbul, built in 1348. It was first a lighthouse, later a prison, and then a place to watch for fires. Today people visit the tower to look out over the city.

pages.text: Huge Palace This palace was built in the late 1400s. Rulers lived here for almost four hundred years. They added new parts to the palace. In 1924, it became a museum. The palace has three big gates and four outdoor spaces with gardens. High walls are all around the outside.
pages.brief: A huge palace stands within high walls, built in the late 1400s. Rulers lived here for almost four hundred years and added new parts. It has three big gates and four outdoor spaces with gardens; in 1924 it became a museum.

pages.text: Grand Museum This huge building was first built as a church in the year 360. When it was built, it was the biggest building in the world. It burned down two times and was built again. It became a mosque in the year 1453. Later, it became a museum. Today, it is a mosque again.
pages.brief: A huge building stands in Istanbul, first built as a church in the year 360, when it was the biggest building in the world. It burned down twice and was rebuilt. It became a mosque in 1453, later a museum, and today is a mosque again.

pages.text: City Square This square was built in the 1700s. All of Istanbul’s water lines met here. Today, the square has shops, hotels, and restaurants. Parades and New Year’s celebrations take place here.
pages.brief: A city square in Istanbul was built in the 1700s, and all of the city’s water lines met here. Today the square has shops, hotels, and restaurants. Parades and New Year’s celebrations take place in this open space.

pages.text: A Trip Back in Time Istanbul is a big city with an interesting history. It brings two continents together and has many wonderful places to visit. Each part of Istanbul has a story to tell. Going there is like taking a trip back in time.
pages.brief: A wide view shows Istanbul as a big city with an interesting history, bringing two continents together. It has many wonderful places to visit. Each part of the city has a story to tell, and going there is like taking a trip back in time.

books.title: The Secret Lives of Snails and Slugs
books.art_why: Real snails, slugs, and their habitats can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Can you guess what walks on one slimy foot? Here’s another clue: this animal has a tongue covered with sharp teeth. Believe it or not, the right answer is a snail or slug. You’ll be amazed when you discover more about these creepy crawlers!
pages.brief: A snail and a slug are shown on damp ground as the answer to a guessing question. One has a single slimy foot; a close view shows a tongue covered with tiny sharp teeth. The two animals look creepy and surprising.

pages.text: Snail and Slug Bodies Snails and slugs are much alike. They belong to the family of animals called mollusks. The and octopuses. All mollusks have soft bodies and no backbones, and most have shells to protect their bodies. Even slugs have a tiny their skin.
pages.brief: A snail and a slug are shown side by side to compare their soft bodies. Both are mollusks with no backbones, and the snail has a shell for protection. A small octopus appears nearby as another mollusk.

pages.text: Snails and slugs are also called gastropods, which means “belly foot.” A snail or slug has one foot, with its head at one end. It seems to walk on its belly, but actually it is crawling on its foot. Snails and slugs have tongues with many rows of tiny sharp teeth.
pages.brief: A snail and a slug crawl on their single belly foot, with their heads at one end. A close view shows their tongues, which have many rows of tiny sharp teeth. They move along the ground.

pages.text: Snails and slugs have four tentacles shaped like arms. At the ends of the top two tentacles are the eyes. These top tentacles are also used to smell. Slugs and snails use their bottom two tentacles for feeling their way along.
pages.brief: A snail and a slug show four tentacles shaped like arms. The top two tentacles end in eyes and are used to smell; the bottom two feel the way along the ground. The animals are shown close up.

pages.text: Slime Snails and slugs move very slowly, gliding along on their single feet. The foot produces slime that helps the snail crawl, like sliding on a bed of jelly. The goo is sticky, so it also helps the animal climb. Slugs and snails drink through their skin, and their slime filters the water.
pages.brief: A snail and a slug glide slowly on a shiny bed of slime made by their feet. The sticky goo helps one climb a wet stem. Water touches their skin, which they drink through as the slime filters it.

pages.text: Slime also helps protect snails and slugs. Birds, snakes, crabs, turtles, and other animals eat snails and slugs. But the slime makes it difficult for these hunters because dinner gets very sticky. Slug slime also tastes awful. This disgusting goo helps stop animals from eating snails and slugs.
pages.brief: A snail and a slug sit covered in sticky, awful-tasting slime. A bird, a snake, a crab, and a turtle are nearby as hunters, but the goo makes the meal difficult and unpleasant. The slime helps protect the animals.

pages.text: Kinds of Snails and Slugs The first snails and slugs probably lived around 600 million years ago. Today, there are around 80,000 kinds of snails and slugs. Some snails and slugs live on land, and others live in water. Many beautiful slugs and snails live in the ocean. Both land and water snails and slugs love wetness. If a snail or slug dries out, it will die.
pages.brief: Many kinds of snails and slugs are shown in wet places. Some live on land, while colorful sea kinds live in the ocean. All of them need wetness; if they dry out, they will die.

pages.text: Snails and slugs can be as tiny as the period on this page, and the largest are the size of rabbits! Snails can have dull, bright, spotted, or striped shells. Many sea slugs are brightly colored with red, blue, purple, silver, or yellow. Most land slugs are brown or green. One slug looks quite a bit like a fruit. It is the banana slug, which lives in the western United States. A banana slug is yellow with black it can grow as big as a banana.
pages.brief: Snails and slugs of many sizes and shell patterns are grouped together, from tiny to rabbit-sized. Bright sea slugs show red, blue, purple, silver, and yellow; land slugs are brown or green. A yellow-and-black banana slug is as big as a banana.

pages.text: The Lives of Snails and Slugs Like bears, land snails and slugs sleep through cold winters. Snails nap in their shells, and slugs sleep in holes they’ve dug in the dirt. In the spring, they come out. They’re very hungry after they wake up, and they need to find plants to eat.
pages.brief: Like bears, a snail naps inside its shell and a slug sleeps in a hole dug in the dirt through the cold winter. In spring they come out very hungry, searching for plants to eat.

pages.text: Snails and slugs spend most of their time searching for food. Land snails and slugs eat live plants, and some eat dead plants, too. They rub their tongues on leaves and stems. Sharp teeth on their tongues grind off bits of plants. Sea snails and slugs eat underwater plants, sponges, and tiny ocean animals.
pages.brief: Land snails and slugs search for food on leaves and stems, rubbing their tooth-covered tongues to grind off bits of plants. Some also eat dead plants. In the ocean, sea snails and slugs eat underwater plants, sponges, and tiny ocean animals.

pages.text: Almost all snails and slugs lay eggs. When each egg hatches, a baby snail or slug crawls out. How long does a snail or slug live? It depends on the type and size. Small snails and slugs usually live about six months, and large snails and slugs might live eight to ten years.
pages.brief: Snail and slug eggs are shown, and a baby snail or slug crawls out as each egg hatches. A small snail or slug is shown beside a large one, hinting at their different lifespans: about six months for small kinds, eight to ten years for large kinds.

pages.text: Conclusion Some snails and slugs can damage crops and gardens, but snails and slugs are very important. They clean up the world by eating dead plants. They provide a source of food for birds and other animals. Now you know all about the secret lives of snails and slugs! Do You Know?
pages.brief: A snail and a slug are in a garden with crops, where they can damage plants. Nearby, they eat dead plants and clean up the world, while a bird watches as a possible hunter. Their secret lives are important.
